    • Technical indicator

    ADX and trend strength

    ADX is an indicator that measures the strength of a trend, not its direction. Two more lines that carry the direction are drawn with it: +DI and −DI. The question it asks is whether price is moving clearly in one direction or going back and forth in a directionless range.

    Which question does ADX answer?

    On a chart we can tell whether price is trending or moving sideways by looking at its highs and lows. ADX reduces this reading to a single number: it measures how consistently price has been extending in one direction recently.

    ADX does not show direction. It rises in a strong uptrend and in a strong downtrend alike. Direction is read from the two directional lines ADX is calculated from: +DI shows the share of upward movement and −DI the share of downward movement. Together the three lines are called the DMI (Directional Movement Index).

    How it is calculated

    1. Find the directional movement. For each candle, up move = this candle's high − the previous high, and down move = the previous low − this candle's low. Whichever is larger, and above zero, counts (+DM or −DM); the other is set to zero.
    2. Find the true range (TR). TR is the largest of three values: high − low, the distance from the high to the previous close, and the distance from the low to the previous close. This is also the basis of ATR.
    3. Smooth over 14 periods and calculate +DI and −DI. +DM, −DM and TR are smoothed over 14 periods with Wilder's method. +DI = 100 × smoothed +DM / smoothed TR; −DI is calculated the same way with −DM.
    4. Calculate DX and ADX. DX = 100 × |+DI − −DI| / (+DI + −DI). ADX is a 14-period Wilder average of DX. That is why it ranges from 0 to 100 and moves slowly.

    Common readings

    • ADX below about 20: often read as a weak or unclear trend, a sideways market.
    • ADX above about 25: often read as a clear trend being in place. Which of +DI and −DI is on top shows the direction.
    • +DI above −DI: upward moves dominate. −DI above +DI: downward moves dominate.
    • ADX at very high levels: the trend is strong, but the move may also have run for a long time. A high ADX on its own does not say the trend will continue.

    The 20 and 25 thresholds are widely used conventions, not rules. Different sources use different thresholds, and settings other than 14 periods can be chosen. The default setting is ADX/DMI 14.

    Rising and falling ADX

    The direction of ADX is read as well as its level. Two ADX readings at the same level can tell different stories.

    ADX rising

    Price is extending more and more consistently in one direction. This can be up or down; the DI lines show which.

    ADX falling

    The trend is losing strength or price is turning sideways. A falling ADX does not mean the trend is reversing, only that it is becoming less consistent.

    ADX low and flat

    Price moves back and forth with no clear direction. The DI lines may cross each other often; crossings say little in this setting.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • How consistently price has been extending in one direction recently
    • Through +DI and −DI, whether upward or downward moves dominate
    • Which side of trend versus sideways the market is closer to

    What it does not prove

    • That the trend will continue, or how long it will last
    • That a trend has started, in good time; because of two stages of smoothing ADX lags price
    • That a falling ADX means a reversal; it only shows strength fading

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    ADX gives a hint about the context in which a support or resistance zone is read. In a sideways market with a low ADX, price often moves between the zones at the edges of the range; reactions at zones are more usual in that setting.

    In a trend moving with a rising ADX, price may be more inclined to move beyond zones. Even so, a breakout is measured not by ADX but by a close beyond the far edge of the zone, read as a band. Because ADX lags, a move out of a zone often shows in price before ADX rises.

    Lag

    ADX smooths the DI lines first and then DX. This double averaging makes the line calm and easy to read, but it also delays it. When a trend starts, it can take several candles or more for ADX to climb above 25; on the 1H chart that means hours, on the 1D chart weeks.

    Often confused with

    • What is a trend?A trend is defined by the sequence of highs and lows and has a direction; ADX only measures how consistent the move is and does not give its direction.
    • Ranges and consolidationA range is price moving between two zones; a low ADX can be a numerical reflection of that, but it does not show the range's boundaries.

    Key points

    • ADX measures a trend's strength, not its direction.
    • +DI and −DI show the direction; the default setting is 14.
    • Below about 20 reads as weak, above 25 as trending; these are conventions.
    • ADX lags; a falling ADX means fading strength, not a reversal.
